interactions.summary: Jiang asks the room for Hannah Arendt's second foundational human action besides making promises; students guess language, love, art, self-reflection, and even lying, while Jiang keeps steering them toward an interpersonal act rather than a solitary capacity.

A student proposes sacrifice, another defines it as giving oneself for another's good, and Jiang says that is close but still too broad before landing on apology and forgiveness as the other distinctly human practice.
Jiang illustrates forgiveness through an everyday collision on the street, then argues that promises and forgiveness together define the basis of a good, just, moral, and divine society.

claims.claim: Jiang, citing Hannah Arendt, says one of the core actions that makes human beings fundamentally human is making promises, because promises bind people to one another and to an imagined shared future.
He identifies forgiveness as the second foundational human action, because humans need to forgive broken promises and ordinary mistakes if social life is going to remain good and just.
Jiang argues that a good, just, moral, and divine society is one in which people feel empowered both to make promises and to forgive one another.

He interprets Beatrice's discussion of vows through Piccarda as a case where a promise to God may be so valuable that ordinary compensation cannot straightforwardly settle it, which makes the moral situation more complex than an absolute rule would suggest.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang defines promising as an act that binds persons to each other and to a jointly imagined future.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you're bonding yourself to the future
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It compresses his Arendt reading into a memorable social ontology of futurity.

signature_moments.moment: Forgiveness arrives not as abstraction but as the everyday act that repairs a bumped body and a broken social thread.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you apologize okay and you forgive
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's concrete hinge between interpersonal failure and moral order.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang reduces the good society to two powers: people can promise, and they can forgive.
signature_moments.source_phrase: these are the two things that make us truly human
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns a Dante exegesis class into a compact theory of moral and political order.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The second Arendtian human action in Jiang's framing: the social power that repairs broken promises and ordinary mistakes so a just society can persist.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-06-18 Jiang reads Dante's vow problem through Hannah Arendt: promises and forgiveness are the two human acts that build a moral society, and Piccarda's case matters because some vows exceed simple replacement or compensation.

uncertainty_notes.note: The ASR renders Hannah Arendt as 'Hannah Rand,' but the reference to The Human Condition and the promise/forgiveness pairing makes the source clearly Hannah Arendt.
